Record Pointing at the Moon (指月錄), Dazhu Huihai section: Dazhu Huihai speaks throughout the answer to a Vimalakirti lecturer; he distinguishes the chapter in which the bodhisattvas explain entry into not-two by using speech to display the speechless.

Senses.Explanation: The gate of not-two is the Vimalakirti case's challenge to meet what is 'not two' without freezing either speech or silence into the answer. Dazhu Huihai reads the case chapter by chapter: the bodhisattvas use speech to display the speechless, Manjusri uses the speechless to display the speechless, and Vimalakirti's silence gathers up the preceding words. Yuanwu Keqin likewise says the verbal positions are swept away all at once. The records refuse to leave the phrase as a settled label. An unnamed monk asks Dongshan Shouchu how to enter the gate and receives 'eyebrows three feet long'; an unnamed official asks Heyi Chaozi what it is and receives another concrete answer. Baiyan Fu says manifesting it would take three lives and sixty aeons. Zhongfeng Mingben can still call Pang's paired warnings a direct route into Vimalakirti's gate. Across these uses, the inherited case supplies the name, while masters turn it back into a question, an answer, an appraisal, and a warning against merely identifying it with muteness.

Senses.Explanation: Not preserve rules is the established second half of ‘great function appears,’ a formula that masters state and then demand be demonstrated in public exchange. An explicitly unnamed questioner asks Chengtian Chuanzong what the formula looks like; Chuanzong answers by raising a surrender flag. Yunmen Wenyan states it to his assembly, and when another explicitly unnamed questioner asks what great function appearing is, Yunmen raises his staff and loudly announces the old buddha’s arrival. Mingjue Cong also gives the formula as an answer before continuing his address. These encounters make ‘rules’ the fixed tracks or established patterns that the displayed function does not retain; the entry does not convert the words into permission for arbitrary conduct. The same wording occurs earlier in Sengcan’s Trust-in-Mind Inscription after motion and stillness are both brought to an end. Zhongfeng Mingben later quotes that line as a lemma and comments on it, preserving a textual lineage distinct from the great-function interview formula. The referent remains one predicate—retaining no fixed pattern—even though it appears in a verse and in interviews. Different genres and readings do not by themselves create different things.

Senses.Explanation: Not deliberating negates the act of mentally considering a stated object or framing a response; the object and time-span must be recovered from its sentence. Dahui Zonggao recounts Mazu considering neither good nor evil, then says deliberation introduces coming and going. Elsewhere Dahui asks what it is when one neither distinguishes nor deliberates, making the negative condition itself part of a public question. Weilin Daopei twice raises Yaoshan’s wording: one address repeats the demand to consider what does not deliberate, and another asks how habitual deliberators could know it. Yun’e Xi specifies past affairs as the object and sets them beside anticipation of the future and lodging in the present. Guxue Zhe supplies the decisive limit: even neither deliberating nor framing an answer can still leave someone in the black-mountain ghost cave. Li Zunxu then asks where the mind goes after not deliberating and receives a situational answer, not a definition of blankness. The phrase occurs 150 times in 81 allowed texts, almost exactly alongside 'not falling into cause and effect' (不落因果, 151); the paired form 'not falling, not being blind' (不落不昧) occurs 86 times. In the recorded Baizhang fox case, an old man asks whether a person of great conduct falls into cause and effect. Baizhang answers, 'not blind to cause and effect' (不昧因果), and the record says the old man was greatly awakened at the words and shed the fox body. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly contrasts the two phrases, while an unnamed monk inside the same commentary objects that even with 'not being blind to cause and effect' the fox body has not yet been shed. Dahui Zonggao preserves the paired questions but answers only by telling the questioner to raise them this way to people. Wumen Huikai asks why 'not falling' brought the fox body and why 'not being blind' shed it, then calls the pair 'two throws, one game' (不落不昧，兩采一賽). Chaozong Tongren rebukes both rejecting 'not falling' and clinging to 'not being blind' as tying oneself without a rope, yet continues by affirming 'not being blind to cause and effect' in his own stated frame. Later records continue asking whether the pair is the same or different. The records preserve competing deployments and questions; this entry does not select a winner among them.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use “not established in written words” as part of the direct-pointing formula associated with Bodhidharma, but their own objections show that it does not amount to a blanket rejection of texts or speech. Yuanwu Keqin gives the familiar sequence—Bodhidharma did not establish written words, directly pointed to the human mind, and disclosed one's nature—then cites the Sixth Patriarch's warning that even the two words “not establish” have already established something. Dahui Zonggao contrasts the extensive canon with single transmission not established in written language and asks why the formula points to one's own mind rather than transmitting verbal subtleties. Mi'an Xianjie and Tianyin Yuanxiu deploy the formula as a concise account of Bodhidharma's coming. Zhongfeng Mingben argues that Sengcan's written Trust in Mind and the no-written-words saying can travel together without contradiction. Juelang Daosheng likewise raises Bodhidharma's use of the Laṅkāvatāra as a challenge and answers that words can point to the mind. Guting Shanmi deliberately calls “not established in written words” a world full of verbal vines and “self-contradiction,” preventing an anti-text slogan from passing as the whole usage.

Senses.Explanation: Layman Pang’s fixed public question—who is not a companion of the ten thousand things?—is repeatedly raised afresh and answered in later records. Literally, not to be or become a companion to the myriad things. The expression is overwhelmingly recorded in the question, 'Who is the one who is not a companion to the myriad things?' The Compendium of the Five Lamps records Layman Pang asking it first of Shitou Xiqian, who covers Pang's mouth, and later of Mazu Daoyi, who answers, 'When you swallow the West River in one mouthful, I will tell you.' Later masters quote Pang's question as a named public case, ask it afresh, and give their own answers. Letan Huaicheng answers 'Guanyin' (觀世音菩薩). Caoshan Benji answers, 'Where did all those many people in Hongzhou city go?' (汝道洪州城裏如許多人甚麼處去). Asked directly, 'Ultimately, what is not being a companion to the myriad things?' (畢竟如何是不與萬法為侶), Yinyuan Longqi answers, 'Passing through a hundred flowers, not one leaf clings to the body' (百花叢裏過，一葉不沾身). Xingkong Zhen answers another fresh raising with 'standing openly revealed' (堂堂獨露). Yuanwu Keqin's instruction says that the ancients called someone 'the person who is not a companion to the myriad things' (古人謂之不與萬法為侶底人). Zhang Jun's preface to Yuanwu's record says that whenever Yuanwu raised this public case, it was already dragging through mud and water and falling into the second meaning. The entry preserves the fixed wording, its named origin, and the answers that the record attaches to it.

Senses.Explanation: In Baizhang's wild-fox case, 'not falling into cause and effect' is the old man's fatal answer; later speakers repeatedly raise and question it against 'not obscuring cause and effect.' An old man who remained after Baizhang's addresses says that in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha he had lived on that mountain. A student asked him, “does a person of great conduct still fall into cause and effect or not?” He answered, “does not fall into cause and effect” (大修行底人還落因果也無？不落因果). The record says this answer was followed by five hundred lives in a wild-fox body. The old man asks Baizhang to give a substitute turning phrase; Baizhang answers, “does not obscure cause and effect” (不昧因果), and the old man awakens at the words. The record continues with the old man's request for a deceased monk's funeral and Huangbo's later question to Baizhang about the case. Wumen asks directly, “Not falling into cause and effect—why did he fall into a wild fox? Not obscuring cause and effect—why was he released from the wild fox?” (不落因果，為甚墮野狐？不昧因果，為甚脫野狐？). Wansong retells the same speaker turns in his commentary. A later master questions a student on the stated difference between falling and not obscuring, while an earlier lamp dialogue rebukes an unnamed monk's “then it does not fall into cause and effect” with “do not make a wild-jackal cry” (莫作野干鳴). The exact phrase occurs 151 times in 82 allowlisted files. Yongjia Collection of the Chan School (禪宗永嘉集): Yongjia's Collection of the Chan School (禪宗永嘉集), in the letter headed Master Yongjia's Reply to Master Lang and signed by Xuanjue, records Yongjia Xuanjue writing that one may roam through mountains and valleys, range through the outskirts, and let the bearing wander freely. Senses.Explanation: To roam at ease is to go or stay freely, without being tied or obstructed by what one meets. The Chan record uses it favorably but also polices the phrase against counterfeit freedom. Yongjue Yuanxian directly defines ‘what is called roaming at ease and ranging freely’ as remaining aloof and unattached amid every false scene, like a bird flying through the sky without the slightest tether and a dragon leaving the sea without the slightest obstruction (所謂逍遙放曠者，乃是於一切妄境，超然不著，如鳥飛空，而毫無所牽繫，如龍出海，而毫無所障礙). In the same address he denies that being tied by sounds, sights, wealth, or power can be called ranging freely and roaming at ease (豈曰放曠逍遙哉). Tianhuang Daowu tells Longtan Chongxin to roam at ease according to his nature, range freely following conditions, exhaust the ordinary mind, and retain no separate superior understanding (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). The Patriarchs' Hall Collection describes Danxia Tianran as delighting in clouds and waters and roaming at ease whether going or staying (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Tianyin Yuanxiu raises his staff and asks whether it is not roaming at ease and unbound; Shiyu Mingfang's community rule rejects taking crazed delusion as roaming at ease (將狂妄作逍遙者). An unnamed monk asks Lumen Fadeng about a person roaming at ease outside things, and Fadeng answers, ‘red and festering all over, unable to be supported’ (如何是逍遙物外底人；遍身紅爛，不可扶持). Yongjia Xuanjue's letter uses the ordinary motion frame ‘roam through mountains and valleys’ (逍遙山谷), which is not the place name Mount Xiaoyao. Juelang Daosheng also uses the word inside the longer title ‘Remarks on Free and Easy Wandering’; that family compound is not a fourth sense of the bare headword.

Senses.Note: The sources preserve no personal name beyond the title Xiaoyao Heshang. This source-attested title is kept exact pending the separate roster expansion. The person sense is distinguishable from the lexical and place senses from its target alone.
